name: Ox bile (cosmetic)

lead:
Ox bile, or ox gall, is the greenish-brown liver secretion of cattle, containing cholesterol, lecithin, taurocholic acid and glycocholic acid. Its degreasing, detergent-like properties made it a traditional ingredient in bile soap.
For appearance, bile-based soaps are used for cleansing, and a cosmetic-industry article describes a related animal ingredient, gallstone, as a skin-conditioning agent that forms a thin film on the skin. No published studies have tested ox bile as a cosmetic skin treatment.

paras: In practice ox gall appears mostly as bile soap sticks and bars applied to fabrics, and as a wetting agent mixed with alcohol for painting and printing. Skin and cosmetic uses are described in marketing texts rather than in clinical sources.

Safety for skin use has not been assessed. A cosmetic-industry article flags possible irritation from residual bile acids if purification is inadequate. Animal-derived origin is a consideration for some users.

web.title: Gallstone: What Is It, Cosmetic Uses, Benefits & Side Effects

chain: Bile salts bind and lift fats and oils
Soap or wash removes grease from the surface
angle.text: Ox bile is used for its detergent action in soaps. Where it is promoted for skin, the stated aim is cleaner, conditioned-looking skin.

lead: Ox gall is bile obtained from cattle, a greenish-brown liquid containing cholesterol, lecithin, taurocholic acid and glycocholic acid.[1] In the 18th century its degreasing properties were noted, and it became useful for removing protein-based stains.[1]

It is an ingredient in bile soap and is mixed with alcohol as a wetting agent in paper marbling, engraving, lithography and watercolour painting.[1] Bile salts are amphipathic, forming micelles around fats, which explains the cleansing action.[2]

Appearance-related use is less documented. A cosmetic-industry article describes bovine gallstone, a related ingredient, as a modern skin-conditioning ingredient whose lipids form a thin breathable film on skin, while noting possible irritation from residual bile acids.[3] No clinical trials of ox bile as a cosmetic have been published.
infobox: Cholesterol, lecithin, taurocholic and glycocholic acids[1]
Stain removal, wetting agent for art[1]
Sold as household soap and art supply

paras: Bile is about 97 to 98 percent water, with bile salts, bilirubin and fats; bile salts form micelles that aid fat absorption in digestion.[2] Ox gall can be mixed with soap to make gall soap, applied to textiles before washing to lift tough stains.[2]

Skin and hair uses are not described in encyclopaedic sources. A cosmetic-industry piece describes a related bovine ingredient, gallstone, as having been valued in traditional medicine and now sold as a skin-conditioning ingredient; this is a marketing source and does not establish efficacy or safety.[3]
The cosmetic-industry article notes possible irritation from residual bile acids if purification was inadequate.[3] No regulator assessments of ox bile as a leave-on skin ingredient were located.

timeline.event: Degreasing properties of ox gall noted; it is used to remove protein stains.[1]
